States the control loop and its graduated form - releases continue while SLOs are met, halt when the budget is spent, with slowing or rolling back releases named as the more effective variant of the on/off technique.

Defines the mechanism verbatim - a quarterly budget derived from the SLO as a clear objective metric that determines how unreliable the service is allowed to be, removing politics from the negotiation, with releases pushing while budget remains.

States the structural conflict the budget resolves - development evaluated on velocity, SRE on reliability, with information asymmetry amplifying the tension - and introduces the error budget as the objective basis for those decisions.

States that queueing delay is invisible to server-side service time and therefore response times must be measured on the client side - the authoritative consumer-visible signal, not a partial internal representation.
Eval and serving gates re-keyed from a rendered view onto the authoritative source signal under production-matching conditions.

A book-ingestion completeness gate observed the converter's self-reported chapter count - the process it gates - and stayed green through under-segmentation; the fix binds reconciliation to the authoritative external signal (published table of contents / PDF outline) in a two-tier gate, measured 23/23 across the catalog.

States that server-side collection is natural but client-side instrumentation is required when server metrics cannot see the user-affecting problem - measuring page-usable time in the browser as the better proxy for what the user experiences - the choose-the-authoritative-collection-point discipline for indicators.

Its errors discussion states that protocol-level success can wrap wrong content and that some failure classes are visible only to end-to-end checks - a gate keyed on the convenient protocol signal passes exactly the failures it exists to catch.
